content: Cutis marmorata is a condition observed in newborn infants when they are exposed to low environmental temperatures. It manifests as a transient, lacy, reticulated vascular pattern on the skin, which appears red and/or blue and typically covers most of the body surface. This vascular phenomenon is an exaggerated physiological vasomotor response that diminishes with age, although it may still be noticeable in some older children. In certain conditions, cutis marmorata can become persistent and more pronounced. These conditions include Menkes disease, familial dysautonomia, Cornelia de Lange syndrome, trisomy 13, and trisomy 18 syndromes. A related condition, cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita, presents with similar clinical features but is more severe. The lesions in this condition are more intense, may follow a segmental distribution, and are persistent. Additionally, they may be associated with dermal tissue loss, epidermal atrophy, and ulceration.
